title.en: Language work for Claribel and the space story: adjectives, merged words, future time, silent letters
Words for a trip through space

text.en: Sven and the crew of a spaceship nearly lose their pet canary Claribel. The language work of this science fiction story teaches us to choose precise adjectives, to build merged words, to talk about the future in seven ways, to pronounce silent letters, to ask for and give advice and to write an article.

keepEnglishTerms: future in the past: was going to, would
merged words: motel, smog, sitcom, vlog, spork, webinar
nagging worry, narrow path, vague plan

text.en:
Adjectives describe nouns, and the right adjective makes a picture. Match nagging with worry, narrow with path, vague with plan, sheepish with look, inexplicable with reason, sluggish with traffic, hushed with voices and delighted with expression.
Nagging means constantly troubling, vague means not clear, inexplicable means impossible to explain, sluggish means slow-moving, hushed means very quiet, and sheepish means embarrassed because you did something silly.
A merged word is made by combining parts of two words. Intercom comes from internal and communication, and brunch comes from breakfast and lunch. Others are motel from motor and hotel, smog from smoke and fog, sitcom from situation and comedy, vlog from video and log, spork from spoon and fork, and webinar from web and seminar.
Verbs can talk about the future in several ways. Will is used for offers, promises, predictions and willingness, as in 'I will help you with your homework'.
The simple present tense is used for the future when it is a fixed schedule: 'Our flight leaves at 10 a.m. tomorrow' and 'My school reopens on 3 January'.
The present progressive tense is used for personal arrangements and fixed plans: 'We are moving into our new house next month' and 'I am visiting my grandparents'.
Going to is used in an informal way for plans and for things we can see are about to happen: 'We are going to get a new motorbike soon'.
The future perfect, will have plus the third form of the verb, says that something will be finished by a certain time: 'The teacher will have completed the portions by next month'. The future progressive, will be plus -ing, says that something will be going on at a moment in the future: 'This time tomorrow I will be relaxing at home'.
Sometimes, when we tell a story about the past, we need to mention something that was still in the future at that time. We say 'you were going to start a new business' and 'I arrived in a town where I would spend the rest of my life'. This is the future in the past.
Silent letters are written but not pronounced. In ballet the t is silent, in whistle the t is silent, in receipt the p is silent, in debris the s is silent, in pneumonia the p is silent, in almond the l is silent, in foreign the g is silent, in island the s is silent, in wreck the w is silent, in aisle the s is silent, in campaign the g is silent and in fasten the t is silent.
To ask for advice we say 'What should I do?' or 'How can I make sure...?' To give advice we say 'I feel you should...' or 'It is best to use...'. These polite phrases are useful for the solar system model and the Chandrayaan-3 quiz situations in the book.
For the writing task, make a web of the uses of the internet, then write an article titled 'The Importance of Internet'. Give a heading, your name, a general introduction in paragraph one, the uses and examples in paragraph two, and a thoughtful closing comment or quote in paragraph three.
For the listening task you hear Monika and Toby, a Martian stranded on Earth, talking about food, school and how he sees. Read the statements first, then tick the correct ones and cross the wrong ones while you listen, and listen again to fill the blanks with the exact words.

prompt.en: Explain two different ways of talking about the future in English with one example each.

requiredIdeas.en: will is used for offers, promises and predictions
the simple present is used for timetables and fixed schedules
the present progressive is used for personal plans
a correct example for each way chosen

commonMisconceptions.en: Using will for every future plan
Using the present progressive for a timetable that nobody planned personally

points.en: Adjectives such as nagging, vague and sheepish describe nouns exactly.
Merged words: intercom, brunch, motel, smog, sitcom, vlog, webinar.
Future forms: will, simple present, present progressive, going to, will have, will be, and the future in the past.
Silent letters: ballet, whistle, receipt, debris, pneumonia, almond, foreign, island, wreck, aisle, campaign, fasten.
An article has a heading, a byline and three paragraphs.
